# 2026-11-25: Where compliance helps, and where it hurts {.unnumbered}

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal" icon="false"}
**Status:** exploratory · **Thread:** T12 · **Checked by:** `tests/test_bench_regimes.py`
:::

**Question.** A compliant element changes what a body can perceive, what it can do and what
it costs. The literature has examples both ways: compliance hides the environment from a
motor, but it also stores and returns energy, protects against shocks and lets a body
conform to the ground. Rather than assume a trade-off, this note maps, across stiffness and
frequency, where compliance helps or hurts each, on two bodies: the book's leg with a
series spring, and a bird whose wings ride on a compliant shoulder.

**Short answer.** There is no single trade-off. What decides is the frequency band of the
task, measured against the resonance of the compliant element, and which part of the body
is asked.

- *Acting.* A series spring raises the ground force the motor can produce per unit torque
  in a band from about a third of the spring's resonance up to the resonance, by up to five
  times. Above the resonance it lowers it, sharply.
- *Withstanding.* The same spring amplifies shocks at the rotor in that band and isolates the
  rotor above it. A soft shoulder does the same for gusts reaching the bird's body: worse
  near its resonance, much better above.
- *Perceiving.* The rotor of a series-elastic leg never perceives the ground better than the
  rigid leg's rotor, at any frequency. The bird's shoulder perceives the gust equally well
  at every shoulder stiffness: its view depends on the shoulder's damping, not its
  stiffness.
- *Paying.* Whether compliance saves energy depends on what is paid for. Motor heat per unit
  ground force falls in the resonance band. Mechanical work per unit ground force never
  falls: the spring's damper only adds losses.

## Setting

*The leg.* The book's rigid leg and series-elastic legs with $k_s$ from 30 to $10^6$ N m/rad
on the ground of @sec-setup ($k_c=10^6$ N/m, $b_c=600$ N s/m), with the Langevin body's
thermal noise. The series spring's resonance, rotor against spring with the link held, is
$f_r=\sqrt{k_s/I_{\rm rot}}/2\pi$. At each frequency the study computes, for each design:

- *perception*: the information density (bits per second per hertz) that the rotor's motion
  holds about the ground force;
- *action*: the ground force per unit motor torque;
- *shock*: the rotor's acceleration per unit ground force;
- *heat*: motor heat per unit squared ground force, for losses proportional to torque
  squared;
- *work*: mechanical power from the motor per unit squared ground force.

*The bird.* The `bird` benchmark: body and wings joined by a shoulder spring $k_s$ (1 to
$10^4$ N/m) with damper $b_s$, lift on the wings with an unsteady gust response, thermal
noise through the shoulder damper. The study computes the shoulder deflection's information
density about the gust, the body's acceleration per unit gust velocity, and the body's
acceleration per unit force of a stroke actuator between wings and body.

Code: `mibook.bench.regimes`.

```{python}
#| label: fig-regimes
#| fig-cap: "Advantage of each compliant design over the stiffest one, at each frequency (log$_{10}$ of the ratio, signed so that blue means the compliant design does better). Top: the leg; the dashed line is the series spring's resonance. Bottom: the bird."
from mibook import figures
figures.fig_regimes();
```

## Results

**The resonance band.** Along the dashed line of @fig-regimes, everything transmitted between
motor and ground is amplified in both directions. The motor gets more ground force per unit
torque (up to 5.1 times the rigid leg's), and a ground impact shakes the rotor harder.
Above the line the spring isolates: little torque reaches the ground and little shock
reaches the rotor. Below about a third of the resonance the spring barely matters for
either. For the soft designs ($k_s\le10^3$) the band where action improves by more than 10%
runs from about $f_r/3$ to $1.1f_r$, and shocks fall by more than 10% from about
$1.25f_r$ upward.

**Perception at the rotor.** Here compliance never helps.

::: {#prp-rotor-never name="A series spring never improves the rotor's view"}
At every frequency, the information density that the rotor of any series-elastic leg holds
about the ground force is at most that of the rigid leg's rotor.
:::

::: {.proof}
The rotor's motion is a function of the whole body's motion, so its information density is at
most the whole body's. In the frequency domain the whole body's density is
$\log_2(1+\text{level}\cdot JD^{-1}J^\top/2\sigma_T^2)$ (the spectral form of @prp-contact),
the same for every design, since $JD^{-1}J^\top=1/b_c$ for all of them. The rigid leg has one
coordinate, so its rotor is its whole body and reaches that value.
:::

The resonance amplifies the rotor's response to the ground force, but it amplifies the
thermal noise reaching the rotor through the series damper by the same or more, so the
signal-to-noise ratio does not rise (@sec-push).

**Paying.** The answer depends on the loss that is paid.

::: {#prp-work-never name="A series spring never saves mechanical work per unit ground force"}
At every frequency, the mechanical power a motor delivers per unit squared ground force is
at least the rigid leg's.
:::

::: {.proof}
For a passive body driven at one port, the mean power delivered equals the mean power
dissipated. The ground dissipates $\frac12b_c\omega^2|y|^2$ for foot motion $y$, and the ground
force is $F_c=(k_c+i\omega b_c)y$, so the ground's share is
$\frac12b_c\omega^2|F_c|^2/|k_c+i\omega b_c|^2$, fixed by $F_c$. The rigid leg has no other
damper. A series-elastic leg adds the series damper's dissipation, which is never negative.
:::

Motor heat per unit ground force behaves like the inverse square of action, so it falls in
the resonance band. A motor whose losses are mostly resistive gains from the spring there.
The mechanical work done on the leg does not.

**The bird's shoulder.** A soft shoulder protects the body from gusts above its resonance
(at 100 Hz a 1 N/m shoulder lets through less than 1% of what the stiffest does) and makes
gusts worse near its resonance. The stroke actuator's authority over the body follows the
same pattern with the opposite sign of benefit: better near resonance, much worse above. At
each frequency, withstanding gusts and acting through the shoulder move together, in
opposite directions of benefit. That is a trade-off, but one that holds band by band, not
across the board.

::: {#prp-shoulder name="The shoulder's view of a gust does not depend on its stiffness"}
In the `bird` model, the information density that the shoulder deflection holds about the
gust depends on the shoulder's damping and on the masses and aerodynamics, not on the
shoulder's stiffness.
:::

::: {.proof}
At frequency $\omega$, write the shoulder's impedance as $Z_s=k_s+i\omega b_s$, the wing's as
$Z_w=-\omega^2m_w+i\omega c$, and let $d$ be the shoulder deflection. The gust acts as a force
$F$ on the wings. The thermal noise of the shoulder damper acts as a pair of forces, $\xi$ on
the wings and $-\xi$ on the body. The equations of motion of body and wings give
$$
  d\,\Delta=\frac{F}{Z_w}+\xi\Big(\frac1{Z_w}-\frac1{\omega^2m_b}\Big),\qquad
  \Delta=1+\frac{Z_s}{Z_w}-\frac{Z_s}{\omega^2m_b}.
$$
(From the body, $-\omega^2m_by_b=Z_sd-\xi$; from the wings, $Z_wy_w=-Z_sd+F+\xi$; and
$d=y_w-y_b$.) The stiffness enters only through $\Delta$, which multiplies signal and noise
alike, so the signal-to-noise ratio at $d$ is
$|F|^2/\big(\E|\xi|^2\,|1-Z_w/\omega^2m_b|^2\big)$ with $\E|\xi|^2=2\sigma_T^2b_s$.
It contains $b_s$ but not $k_s$.
:::

This mirrors the leg's whole-body result, where the information is set by the contact damper
alone (@prp-contact). In both cases a spring changes how strongly the signal and the noise
reach a coordinate, but changes both by the same factor.

## What this means

Compliance is neither good nor bad for action or perception. For action, it helps in a band
set by its resonance and hurts above it. For withstanding the environment, the reverse. For
perception at a part beyond the spring, it can only hurt or leave things unchanged, because
it adds a noisy path. A spring that only adds stiffness, as in the shoulder, changes nothing
about what that coordinate perceives. Whether it saves energy depends on whether the losses
are in the motor or in the mechanism. A design question about compliance therefore needs the
task's band, the part asked, and the loss model stated.

*What is not settled here.* The models are linear. Compliance in real legs also matters
through nonlinear effects this study cannot see: energy return over a stance phase, impact
transients beyond linear response, and terrain conformation (the many-legged and tentacle
benchmarks are the places to look). Empowerment over a finite horizon, computed in the
[comparison note](2026-11-25-comparison.qmd), gives the same answer as the action map here:
on the leg it peaks at an intermediate stiffness.
